title: Physical Therapy Abbreviations List
summary: A practical list of physical therapy abbreviations for exams, history, plans, and weight bearing, grouped by where they appear in a note, plus the pairs that cause mix-ups.
body_markdown:
Physical therapy abbreviations are shortened medical terms and phrases used in patient notes to write down findings, interventions, and the plan of care. They help physical therapists save time when documenting a visit. However, no official list of physical therapy abbreviations exists, and some abbreviations vary from one clinic to the next.


Some common physical therapy abbreviations include MMT (manual muscle testing), AROM (active range of motion), WNL (within normal limits), PLOF (prior level of function), POC (plan of care), ther ex (therapeutic exercise), and neuro re-ed (neuromuscular re-education).


These abbreviations exist for a practical reason: the same phrases recur for every patient, and notes are often written between patients rather than after.


## Exam and measurement abbreviations


The following abbreviations are common in the objective section of outpatient physical therapy notes, though specific wording may vary by clinic.


Abbreviation Meaning How it appears in a note


ROM Range of Motion Cervical ROM limited in rotation, R more than L.


AROM Active Range of Motion AROM shoulder flexion 0-150°.


PROM Passive Range of Motion PROM knee extension lacks 5° of full extension.


MMT Manual Muscle Test MMT hip abduction 4-/5 R, 5/5 L.


WNL Within Normal Limits Sensation WNL to light touch, both lower extremities.


WFL Within Functional Limits Lumbar ROM WFL; pain at end range of flexion.


NPRS Numeric Pain Rating Scale NPRS 6/10 at worst, 2/10 at best.


SLR Straight Leg Raise SLR positive on the R at 45°.


TTP Tender to Palpation TTP over the lateral epicondyle.


BLE / BUE Bilateral Lower / Upper Extremities Strength 5/5 BLE.


These abbreviations are not universal. Some clinics use slightly different abbreviations and combinations of terms. For example, AROM and PROM describe who produces the motion, and some clinics add AAROM for active-assisted range of motion. In many clinics, WNL and WFL are used interchangeably, while others keep them apart: WNL means a normal value, and WFL means enough motion or strength for the patient's daily tasks, even if below normal.


MMT depends on the scale. Most clinics use the 0 to 5 scale, but some add plus and minus grades (4-/5, 4+/5). MMT is written as a fraction (for example, 4/5), while pain is usually recorded on a 0 to 10 scale.


Side is written in different ways too. Some notes use R and L, others Rt and Lt, and "both sides" can appear as B, BL, or bil. Writing the side out in full removes any doubt about which limb was measured. Range of motion is recorded in degrees, and the degree sign is often left out.


## Medical history and plan abbreviations


After the objective exam, you'll find several abbreviations throughout the patient's history, assessment, and plan. Learn these in context, because several look similar but mean different things.


Abbreviation Meaning How it appears in a note


CC Chief Complaint CC: R knee pain with stairs for 3 weeks.


PMH Past Medical History PMH: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, L TKA in 2022.


H/o History of H/o L ankle sprain in 2023; no prior surgery.


PLOF Prior Level of Function PLOF: independent with community ambulation, no assistive device.


Dx Diagnosis Dx: R patellofemoral pain syndrome.


STG Short-Term Goal STG: patient will climb 12 stairs with a reciprocal pattern in 3 weeks.


LTG Long-Term Goal LTG: patient will return to recreational running in 12 weeks.


POC Plan of Care POC: 2x/week for 6 weeks, ther ex, manual therapy, HEP.


NDT Neurodevelopmental Treatment NDT techniques used to facilitate weight shift in standing.


PN Progress Note PN completed; goals updated, POC continued.


HEP Home Exercise Program HEP issued and reviewed; patient demonstrated correct performance.


BID Twice a Day HEP BID: 2 sets of 10 repetitions.


D/C Discharge or Discontinue D/C to independent HEP. (Discharge) / D/C ice after session. (Discontinue)


KX Medicare modifier for therapy above the yearly threshold KX modifier applied; medical necessity documented in the note.


### Commonly confused pairs


**STG vs LTG:** STG is a goal for the next few weeks, while LTG is the goal for the end of the episode of care.


**AROM vs PROM:** AROM is motion the patient produces on their own, such as lifting the arm. PROM is motion the therapist produces while the patient stays relaxed. Some clinics write ROM for both, so always check your clinic's habits.


**BID vs 2x/week:** BID comes from the Latin *bis in die* and means twice a day, which is how often the patient does the HEP. Visit frequency is written per week instead, such as 2x/week, so don't read BID as two visits.


**D/C:** Pay close attention to D/C. Context usually makes the meaning clear, but on its own, D/C can be ambiguous. In some notes it means discharge; in others, discontinue.


**PN and KX:** In outpatient physical therapy, PN generally means "progress note." Elsewhere in a medical record, it can mean something else, so spell it out on documents that leave the clinic. KX is the modifier Medicare uses for therapy above a yearly threshold; the threshold changes every year, so check the current amount on the[CMS therapy services page](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/therapy-services) .


## Weight-bearing and assistance abbreviations


This group of abbreviations requires the most caution. A single misreading can lead to a serious error, such as a post-operative patient putting full weight on a leg that should bear none, or walking without the help they need, any of which can harm a patient.


Abbreviation Meaning How it appears in a note


NWB Non-Weight Bearing NWB L lower extremity, ambulates with axillary crutches.


TTWB / TDWB Toe-Touch / Touch-Down Weight Bearing TTWB R lower extremity per surgeon's protocol.


PWB Partial Weight Bearing PWB R lower extremity with a rolling walker.


WBAT Weight Bearing as Tolerated WBAT both lower extremities.


FWB Full Weight Bearing FWB cleared at 6 weeks post-op.


I Independent I with bed mobility and transfers.


Mod I Modified Independent Mod I with ambulation using a cane.


SBA Stand-By Assist SBA for stairs.


CGA Contact Guard Assist CGA for gait on uneven surfaces.


Min A / Mod A / Max A Minimal / Moderate / Maximal Assist Min A for sit-to-stand from a low chair.


AD Assistive Device Ambulates 300 ft with AD (rolling walker).


RW / SPC Rolling Walker / Single-Point Cane Progressed from RW to SPC.


### Abbreviations that are easy to misread


The weight-bearing abbreviations NWB, TTWB, PWB, WBAT, and FWB need extra care. When handwritten or typed in a hurry, a dropped "N" turns NWB into WB, which reads as the opposite instruction. Similarly, the assistance levels Min A, Mod A, and Max A look alike at a glance and are easy to swap.


## Abbreviations patients shouldn't see: writing them out in discharges


The physical therapy note is written in shorthand. The discharge instructions, on the other hand, are what the patient takes home, so they should be written in plain language anyone can understand.


Here's the same visit written both ways.


In the physical therapy note:


note


Pt reports 2/10 pain. AROM knee flex 0-125°, MMT quads 5/5. LTG met. D/C to I HEP 1x/day. Return PRN.


_


On the discharge:


discharge


You reported mild pain today, 2 out of 10. Your knee now bends well, and your thigh muscles tested at full strength. You have met your long-term goal. You are discharged from therapy and should continue your home exercise program on your own once a day. Contact the clinic if you have concerns or if your symptoms change.


_


Writing a discharge means decoding the physical therapy note into home exercise instructions, precautions, activity guidance, and follow-up, which takes time. It's the same routine, patient after patient. Retyping "perform each exercise once a day" or "contact the clinic if you have concerns" takes only a few seconds each time, but it adds up to minutes that clinical staff could spend on patient care.
